transcript:
Header:
Date: 2026-03-22
Time: 15:00 PDT
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Liam O'Connor (Redwood SE), Priya Shah (Arctera), Markus Li (Arctera), Ruth Caldwell (Arctera)
Shared artifacts: Arctera infra diagram (customer), Redwood dedicated overview deck: https://redwood.com/deck/dedicated-overview, Benchmark template link: https://redwood.com/benchmarks/template

Auto-generated Summary (optional):
Arctera is evaluating a hybrid approach: reserve dedicated on-prem/GPU pools for isolation-sensitive workloads with the ability to burst to Redwood hosted for peak traffic. Primary concerns: tenant isolation, deterministic latency (95th/99th), predictable monthly cost, and data residency/SOC2 controls. They want a clear sizing playbook and a runbook for failover/burst that minimizes cold-start latency and cost.

Transcript body:
[00:00] Maya (Redwood AE): hey everyone, thanks for joining — I'm Maya from Redwood, with Liam who is our SE, we're excited to learn a bit about Arctera's needs. quick intro, please?
[00:18] Priya (Arctera): sure, hi, I'm Priya, head of MLOps. we run their inference platform for personalized search + rerank. we have a mixed fleet, on-prem K8s with A100 nodes and a few T4s for low-cost tasks, um, looking to understand dedicated options and how a burst strategy would work.
[00:38] Markus (Arctera): Markus here, infra. primary concern is isolation — we can't have noisy neighbor impact across tenant workloads. we also want the ability to, like, spin up extra capacity during promo events and traffic spikes without permanent over-provisioning.
[00:56] Ruth (Arctera): and from product, we need predictable latency at 95th, and cost targets, otherwise the product roadmap stalls.
[01:10] Liam (Redwood SE): cool. thank you. quick clarifying question: when you say "isolation", do you mean hardware-level isolation per tenant or just node pools with network/namespace isolation?
[01:24] Priya: hardware-level if possible. we have compliance rules for certain customers that require dedicated GPUs and no shared instance. on the other hand, for non-sensitive customers we can consolidate.
[01:38] Maya: good — that's exactly the mix we see. Redwood Dedicated supports reserved GPU pools you can pin to tenant groups and then a separate general pool. you can also configure burst policies to fall back to Redwood hosted endpoints when dedicated capacity is exhausted.
[01:55] Markus: how fast does that fallback happen? latency of, like, user-facing features is critical.
[02:05] Liam: typically routing and failover can be configured for sub-second steering once capacity is known to be exhausted, but you have to design for model compatibility — we maintain a catalog of compatible model variants. if the customer pins to a 8-bit quantized variant on dedicated, we can fall back to a hosted variant with similar perf characteristics. there are caveats, cold-starts, and initial KV cache warm-up.
[02:32] Priya: KV cache?
[02:34] Liam: K V cache — sometimes transcribed as K V cash, sorry — the key-value cache we use for autoregressive workloads. warm caches are important for tail latency. if you pop over to hosted during a spike, the cache will need to rebuild unless you use prefix caching or a shared cache strategy.
[02:50] Ruth: we have long-context prompts and heavy session state — will that make the hosted fallback unacceptable?
[02:59] Liam: it can. for long context and big KV working sets, dedicated nodes with persistent KV caches are ideal. for bursts we recommend fallbacks only for stateless or trimmed sessions, or you can implement a hybrid where you route reads to cached dedicated nodes and only overflow new requests to hosted, depending on your SLOs.
[03:20] Maya: can we go over your traffic profile so we can sketch a sizing playbook?
[03:25] Priya: sure. baseline qps is around 400 reqs/sec during normal hours, average token generation per request is 120 tokens. peaks during product launches reach ~1800-2200 reqs/sec for about 20-30 minutes, twice a quarter.
[03:46] Markus: also a seasonal big spike possibility — Black Friday style, could be 5x baseline but for an hour.
[03:55] Liam: okay that's helpful. rough math — 400 rps baseline with 120-token gen, depending on model (say a 13B), you'd need X GPUs for baseline; peaks are about 5x. reserved capacity should cover baseline + some buffer; recommended burst policy is to allow autoscale on dedicated up to limit and then overflow to hosted with pre-warmed model variants.
[04:18] Priya: can you be more concrete about "X GPUs"?
[04:21] Liam: absolutely — we'll run a sizing spreadsheet but as a rough starting point, baseline might be covered by 8 A100s for low-latency 13B q4-style quant, peak of 2k rps would need 40+ GPUs if served purely on dedicated without batching or specialized kernels. with continuous batching and KV caching you can reduce that significantly.
[04:44] Maya: important to call out: model selection and quantization change the numbers a lot. we will send you a spreadsheet where you can flip model size and quant profile to see GPU counts and estimated monthly cost.
[04:55] Ruth: what about bursting cost? if we burst to hosted for 30 minutes, is it cheaper than keeping extra reserved GPUs idle?
[05:05] Maya: usually yes — burst-to-hosted is cheaper for infrequent spikes because you only pay for consumed tokens/capacity during the burst. reserved always costs the committed monthly fee. there is also a hybrid reserved+burst pricing where reserved units can bank short-term burst credits. we'll include options in the spreadsheet.
[05:23] Markus: we also need to ensure data residency — some inference requests reference PII and need to stay in our region. can hosted handle region restrictions?
[05:33] Liam: Redwood Hosted has regional endpoints; you can configure routing by region. for strict residency and compliance, Redwood Private (VPC) or Dedicated on-prem with private control plane is ideal — those give you full data-plane isolation and KMS control.
[05:48] Priya: our security must-haves: SOC2, SSO (SAML), customer-managed KMS, audit logs for model access, and network policies. do you support HSM?
[05:59] Maya: we support KMS integrations and HSM-backed keys for Private deployments; audit logs and token-level tracing are in Console. we'll share the SOC2 summary and KMS integration guide.
[06:12] Ruth: one more thing — our infra team worries about vendor lock-in and migration complexity. what does the Private offering look like?
[06:22] Liam: Redwood Private gives you a customer-managed control plane and optional on-prem packaging; the API remains the same so migration is mainly around provisioning the serving runtime on your infra and syncing model artifacts. for portability, we recommend containerized model artifacts and keeping eval/validation assets in your repo.
[06:40] Priest? [crosstalk]
[06:42] Priya: sorry, "Priya" — just noting: we run jobs on preemptible nodes for batch, but inference must be on non-preemptible. can Dedicated designate non-preemptible GPU pools?
[06:52] Liam: yes, Dedicated pools are non-preemptible. you can reserve them or make them auto-scaled but we can mark them as non-preemptible for compliance.
[07:02] Markus: operationally, how are rollouts handled? can we do canary vs all-at-once?
[07:09] Maya: Redwood Console supports canary rollouts, A/B tests, and automatic fallback policies based on error rates or latency regressions. you can pin traffic percentages or route by customer segments.
[07:23] Priya: benchmark question — will you run benchmarks with our prompts or do we run them?
[07:29] Liam: we can do both. recommended flow: you provide representative prompts and a sample dataset, we run a controlled benchmark on the dedicated nodes and hosted fallbacks, and we share the logs + token-level latency breakdowns. that will show warm vs cold cache behavior.
[07:45] Ruth: any gotchas with batching? we rely on low tail latency, we've seen batching increase 99th.
[07:51] Liam: yes batching increases throughput but can affect tail latency. Redwood implements dynamic batching with latency caps — you can configure per-route latency SLOs so batching only accumulates for a short interval. Also continuous KV caching reduces time per token, which helps tail.
[08:09] Priya: what about GPU types? we have A100s on-prem; Redwood hosted uses a mix of Hopper and Ampere. are there perf differences we should expect?
[08:20] Liam: yes, Hopper usually gives better throughput for FP16 kernels; Ampere/A100 is close. kernel selection is important — our runtime selects kernels based on model architecture and sequence length. we'll show perf profiles for similar models during the benchmark.
[08:33] Maya: quick note on pricing: dedicated is typically a reserved monthly fee per GPU or pool; hosted is per-token. we can model both approaches in the spreadsheet for your traffic trace.
[08:44] Markus: ok, so next, we want a runbook for failover — what does that look like in practice?
[08:50] Liam: simple pattern: primary route to dedicated pool; if CPU/GPU utilization > threshold or queue latency > X ms for Y seconds, route overflow to hosted variant via Smart Routing. step two: if model mismatch is material, rewrite prompts to trimmed context or shed non-critical features. we also suggest a short-circuit route for emergency fallback which serves a fast small model to preserve UX.
[09:14] Priya: interesting, that "small model emergency" route — do you have examples?
[09:18] Liam: yes, many customers maintain a distilled 3B model that approximates responses; it's not perfect but maintains low latency for essential flows while you scale.
[09:28] Ruth: operationally, who monitors and runs the initial burst? our SREs or Redwood?
[09:33] Maya: depends on the engagement. for Dedicated, typical model: Arctera runs SRE ops, Redwood provides on-call support and runbooks. for Private deployments we offer an enterprise ops package where Redwood runs the control plane and supports on-call.
[09:49] Priya: for audit reasons we probably want Arctera SRE to own the process but Redwood on-call to assist.
[09:55] Maya: makes sense.
[09:57] [10:00] [Speaker labels get a bit noisy]
[10:05] Markus: can you walk through a sample SLO rule for overflow? like exact thresholds?
[10:12] Liam: example: if p95 request latency > 300 ms for 60 seconds OR GPU queue length > 70% for 45 seconds, trigger overflow to hosted. you can tune these. we also recommend health checks at route level so you avoid thrashing.
[10:29] Priya: that 300 ms is tight for us; our teams push for 200 ms p95. is that feasible?
[10:36] Liam: feasible with the right model and kernel; more GPUs and lower batching windows. we'll show tradeoffs in the sizing sheet.
[10:44] Ruth: will the console show token-level cost during bursts so we can estimate 30-minute event cost?
[10:51] Maya: yes Console gives token-level cost and per-route dashboards; we can also run a simulated cost projection from your traces.
[10:58] Markus: curious about data plane encryption and KMS key rotation — is that supported for both Dedicated and Private?
[11:05] Liam: yes, Private supports customer-managed KMS and key rotation policies. Dedicated hosted in Redwood-managed infra can integrate with your KMS via customer key material in supported clouds, but on-prem gives full control.
[11:18] Priya: any network requirements for on-prem Dedicated?
[11:21] Liam: minimal outbound control-plane connectivity for management (if you pick managed control plane), but full VPC/private connectivity is supported. we'll include a network requirements doc.
[11:31] Maya: starting to run short on time — quick recap and next steps?
[11:35] Priya: yes please.
[11:36] Maya: we'll: 1) send the dedicated sizing/pricing spreadsheet; 2) run a benchmark template once you share prompts; 3) share SOC2 + KMS + VPC docs; 4) schedule a 1-hr benchmark run wk of 3/30. anyone disagree?
[11:52] Ruth: sounds good.
[11:53] Markus: good.
[11:55] Priya: will you include a suggested playbook for overflow rules and the small-model emergency route?
[12:00] Liam: yes, we'll provide a suggested playbook and example SLO thresholds.
[12:06] Maya: awesome. thanks everyone. we'll follow up with the spreadsheet and booking link.
[12:12] [meeting close]
